title: 1 · I want, I can
intro: We'll build real sentences from two little engine words — no memorising lists. Take your time, say each answer out loud before you reveal it.

steps.teach: "Quiero" = I want. Spanish's plain "to …" form of a verb ends in -ar, -er or -ir. "hablar" = to speak (the h is silent: ah-BLAHR). Stick it straight onto quiero.
"comer" = to eat. Think "comestibles".
"Puedo" = I can. Same family as "potent" and "possible".
To ask a question you change nothing — just lift your voice at the end. In writing, Spanish warns you at the start with an upside-down ¿.
"no" = not. It sits right in front of the verb — English "I do not" without the "do".
"ahora" = now. The h is silent: ah-OH-rah. Extra words go on the end.
"venir" = to come. There's your -ir ending.

steps.prompt: I don't want to come now

title: 2 · I have to — and how to say "it"
intro: One more engine word, and the little trick Spanish uses to hook "it" onto a verb.

steps.teach: "Tengo que" = I have to. Literally "I have that", then the plain verb.
"ir" = to go. Just two letters.
"hacer" = to do, to make (silent h: ah-SEHR). "algo" = something.
Now the trick. "lo" = it. On a plain verb it hooks onto the END as one word: hacer + lo = hacerlo.
"ver" = to see. Think "visible".
You can also put lo in front of the engine word instead. Both are completely normal.
steps.prompt: I want to see it — the other way round

steps.teach: "comprar" = to buy.

title: 3 · I have, I am — tengo, soy, estoy
intro: Spanish has two verbs for "to be". It sounds like double the work; really it's an extra piece of meaning you get for free. Soy is what you are. Estoy is how and where you are right now.

steps.teach: "Tengo" on its own = I have. "tiempo" = time (think "tempo").
Spanish has hunger, thirst and years where English is them. "hambre" = hunger. No -o/-a to worry about either.
"años" = years. "treinta" = thirty.
"Soy" = I am — for what you are: name, job, where you're from, what you're like. The label.
No "a" before a job. A man says profesor, a woman profesora.
"Estoy" = I am — for where you are and how you are right now. The state, not the label.
"bien" = well, fine.
Same adjective, different verb, different meaning: "aburrido" with estoy = bored.
…and with soy = boring.
steps.hint: soy = what you are, so this is a confession

steps.teach: One more: estoy lista = I'm ready; soy lista = I'm clever.

title: 4 · you, he, she, we
intro: So far everything has been "I". Now we change the end of the verb and get everyone else for free.

steps.teach: For "you" (a friend), swap the -o for -es: quiero → quieres.
steps.hint: no word for "you" needed — the ending says it

steps.teach: puedo → puedes.
For he or she, drop the -s: quiere, puede. Add él (he) or ella (she) only when it isn't clear who.
For "we", the ending is -mos — and the stem goes back to its plain shape: queremos, podemos.
For "you all" and "they", add -n to the he/she form: quieren, pueden. In Latin America "ustedes" is the only plural you — friends, family, anyone.
steps.prompt: Do you guys want to eat?

steps.teach: tengo follows the same pattern: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
estar too: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están. "¿Dónde?" = where.

title: 5 · where, what, when, why
intro: A handful of question words. Once you have these you can get through a day in Mexico City on your own.

steps.teach: "¿Dónde?" = where. Where something is always takes estar.
"¿Qué?" = what. Say KEH — qu is always k.
"¿Cuándo?" = when.
"¿Por qué?" = why — literally "for what".
The answer is the same two words glued together, no accent: porque = because.
"¿Cómo?" = how. "haces" = you do.
steps.hint: lo goes in front of a normal verb

steps.teach: "¿Quién?" = who. It takes the he/she form, like English "who wants".
"¿Cuánto?" = how much. "cuesta" = it costs.

steps.prompt: What do we have to do?

title: 6 · and, but, eat, drink
intro: The joining words, and the two verbs you'll use at every meal.

steps.teach: "y" = and, said "ee". "tomar" = to drink (and to take); tomar algo = have a drink. Beber exists, but tomar is what people say.
steps.prompt: I want to eat and have a drink

steps.teach: "pero" = but. One r, a light tap — perro with a rolled rr is a dog.
steps.prompt: I want to eat, but I can't

steps.teach: "agua" = water (think "aquarium").
"o" = or.
"también" = too, as well. "yo" = I, added here for emphasis.
"tampoco" = not either.
"nada" = nothing. Spanish happily doubles its negatives: not I-want nothing.
"como" = I eat — the same -o as quiero and puedo. "carne" = meat (think "carnivore").
"pagar" = to pay. Every verb takes -mos for "we".
steps.prompt: We eat and drink, but we don't pay
steps.answer: Comemos y tomamos, pero no pagamos.

title: 7 · -o or -a: the, a, and speaking as yourself
intro: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the last letter usually tells you which. The same -o/-a then shows up on almost any word you use to describe yourself — so a man and a woman say "I'm tired" differently. English gives you no warning about this; get it now and half of Spanish falls into place.

steps.teach: "el" = the, for -o words. "la" = the, for -a words.
libro ends in -o, so el.
"un" / "una" = a.
Plural: add -s, and the "the" becomes los or las.
Now you. "cansado" = tired, said by a man.
One letter, and a woman is speaking.
"contento / contenta" = happy, pleased.
Words ending in -e or a consonant don't change at all.
A group: -as if they're all women…
…and -os if there's a single man in it.

title: 8 · my, your — and the trap in "su"
intro: English possessives tell you who owns the thing: his sister, her brother, their house. Spanish "su" covers all of those at once — and a formal "your" too. It's the most reliable mix-up an English speaker makes.

steps.teach: "mi" = my, "tu" = your. They don't change for masculine and feminine.
Only plural changes them: mis, tus.
Now the trap. "su" = his, her, its, their — and the formal your. It says something is owned, not who owns it.
Same word.
And again.
When it really matters, Spanish spells it out after the thing: de él (his), de ella (hers).
steps.prompt: her house — making it clear it's hers, not his

steps.teach: "nuestro / nuestra" = our. This one does agree — with the thing owned, never the owner.

title: 9 · Me llamo: verbs that loop back
intro: Lots of everyday Spanish verbs point back at the person doing them: I call myself, I get myself up, I take myself off. Once you see the little me/te/se, they stop looking strange.

steps.teach: "Me llamo" = my name is — literally "I call myself". me = myself.
te = yourself. Literally "how do you call yourself?"
se = himself, herself, themselves.
"levantarse" = to get up (to raise yourself). "a las siete" = at seven.
With a plain verb, me hooks onto the end, just like lo did.
"irse" = to leave — to take yourself off. voy = I go.
"ya" = already. vas = you go.
"quedarse" = to stay. nos = ourselves.
"sentirse" = to feel. Think "sentiment".

title: 10 · Me gusta: I like it
intro: Spanish doesn't say "I like pizza". It says "pizza pleases me". Turn it around in your head and the whole thing falls into place.

steps.teach: "Me gusta" = it pleases me. Think "gusto".
The thing that pleases goes after.
If the thing is plural, the verb is too: gustan — the dogs please me.
te = to you.
le = to him or to her.
With an activity, use the plain verb. "bailar" = to dance.
"me encanta" = I love it — it enchants me. For things, not people.

title: 11 · What I did yesterday
intro: Spanish has a one-word past for finished actions, and Latin America uses it for nearly everything — "I ate" and "I've eaten" alike. Good news: it never changes for whether you're a man or a woman.

steps.teach: -ar verbs: hablar → hablé = I spoke. The stress jumps to the end.
-er and -ir verbs: comer → comí. "demasiado" = too much.
"ayer" = yesterday. lo goes in front of a normal verb.
For you: -aste for -ar verbs, -iste for -er/-ir verbs.
For he or she: -ó or -ió. That accent is everything: hablo = I speak, habló = he spoke.
"fui" = I went — and also I was. ir and ser share their past.
"hice" = I did, "hiciste" = you did.

title: 12 · What I'm going to do
intro: The future the easy way: exactly like English "I'm going to".

steps.teach: "Voy a" + plain verb = I'm going to.
voy, vas, va, vamos, van.
"Vamos a" doubles as "let's".
"mañana" = tomorrow. "trabajar" = to work.

steps.prompt: I'm not going to do it

steps.teach: As before, lo can sit in front of the engine word instead.
steps.prompt: I'm going to buy it — with lo in front
What are you going to do?

title: 13 · Numbers and the time
intro: Enough numbers to tell the time, say your age, and fix when to meet.

steps.teach: uno, dos, tres — OO-noh, DOHS, TREHS.
cuatro (4), cinco (5), seis (6), siete (7), ocho (8), nueve (9), diez (10).
Literally "what hour is it?" The h is silent.
Hours are plural, with "the": son las + number.
Only one o'clock is singular.
"y media" = and a half. "y cuarto" = quarter past.
"a las" = at.
"veinte" = twenty. Remember: you have years.
